What are the eight bases for views?
The aggregates are a basis for views; ignorance is a basis for views; contact is a basis for views; perception is also...
The basis for views is a basis for views; applied thought is also a basis for views; improper attention is also a basis for views;
evil friends are also a basis for views; the voice of another is also a basis for views.
The aggregates are the cause, the aggregates are the condition, as a basis for views in the sense of origination.
In this way, the aggregates are also a basis for views.
Ignorance is the cause, ignorance is the condition; in the sense of arising dependent upon a basis for views, ignorance too is a basis for views.
Contact is the cause, contact is the condition, by way of being the source for the standpoint of views;
thus, contact too is a standpoint for views.
Perception is the cause, perception is the condition, by way of being the source for the standpoint of views.
In this way, perception (*saññā*) is also a basis for views (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*).
Thought (*vitakka*) is the cause, thought is the condition, for the basis of views in the sense of origination—
in this way, thought too is a basis for views.
Improper attention is the cause, improper attention is the condition for a ground for views in the sense of origination;
thus, improper attention is also a ground for views.
An evil friend is the cause, an evil friend is the condition for a ground for views in the sense of origination.
In this way, an evil friend is also a ground for views.
The voice of another is the cause, the voice of another is the condition, for the arising of a ground for views in the sense of origination—
in this way, the voice of another is also a ground for views.
These are the eight bases of views.
What are the eighteen obsessions of views?
That which is a view, a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views;
The fetter of views, the dart of views, the confinement of views, the obstruction of views,

the bond of views, the precipice of views, the underlying tendency of views, the fever of views, the burning of views, the knot of views, the clinging to views, the dogmatic insistence on views, and the misapprehension by views.

These are the eighteen obsessions of views. What are the sixteen views? The view of gratification, the view of self, wrong view, the view of a personal entity, the eternalist view based on a personal entity, [the annihilationist view based on a personal entity, the view of selfhood, the view of clinging to selfhood, the view of selfhood in what is not self, the view of selfhood in what is not a self, the view that "I am," the view that "mine," the view that "I am this," the view that "this is mine," the view that "I shall be," and the view that "this is my self"]. These are the sixteen views. What are the two views? The view of existence and the view of non-existence. These are the eighteen obsessions of views. What are the nine underlying tendencies? The underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to pride, and the underlying tendency to envy. These are the nine underlying tendencies. What are the seven latent dispositions? The latent disposition to sensual lust, the latent disposition to aversion, the latent disposition to views, the latent disposition to doubt, the latent disposition to conceit, the latent disposition to lust for existence, and the latent disposition to ignorance. These are the seven latent dispositions. What are the five higher fetters? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These are the five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust, ill will, and envy. These are the five lower fetters. What are the four taints? The taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. These are the four taints. What are the four nutriments?

Physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These are the four nutriments. What are the four kinds of clinging? Clinging to sensuality, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self. These are the four kinds of clinging. What are the four kinds of identity view? "Form is self," "form is distinct from self," "self possesses form," or "form is in self. This is the first kind of identity view. "Feeling is self," "feeling is distinct from self," "self possesses feeling," or "feeling is in self. This is the second kind of identity view. "Perception is self," "perception is distinct from self," "self possesses perception," or "perception is in self. This is the third kind of identity view. "Volitional formations are self," "volitional formations are distinct from self," "self possesses volitional formations," or "volitional formations are in self. This is the fourth kind of identity view. These are the four kinds of identity view. What are the four perversions? The perversion of perception, the perversion of thought, the perversion of view, and the perversion of conduct. These are the four perversions. What are the four foundations of mindfulness? Herein, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four right endeavors? Herein, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, development, and fulfillment by cultivation of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. These are the four right endeavors. What are the four bases of psychic power? Herein, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. These are the four bases of psychic power. What are the four jhānas? Herein, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. These are the four jhānas. What are the four immaterial attainments? Herein, by completely transcending forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking: "Space is infinite," a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. By completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking: "Consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking: "There is nothing," he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. By completely transcending the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are the four immaterial attainments. What are the four analytical knowledges? Herein, a bhikkhu is skilled in meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in phrasing, and skilled in the sequence of exposition. These are the four analytical knowledges. What are the four discriminations? Discrimination of meaning, discrimination of Dhamma, discrimination of language, and discrimination of eloquence. These are the four discriminations. What are the four paths? The path leading to hell, the path leading to the animal realm, the path leading to the sphere of afflicted spirits, and the path leading to heaven. These are the four paths. What are the four fruits of the ascetic life? The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship. These are the four fruits of the ascetic life. What are the four noble lineages? Herein, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, any kind of almsfood, any kind of lodging, and any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. These are the four noble lineages. Description of the View of Gratification (*assāda-diṭṭhi*):
Through which thirty-five modes is there adherence regarding the view of gratification?
The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on form: this is the gratification of form—this is a dogmatic adherence and a wrong view.
A wrong view is not the gratification; the gratification is not the wrong view.
View is one thing, gratification is another.
That which is the view and that which is the gratification—
this is called the view of gratification.
The view of gratification is wrong view, a failure of view.
A person endowed with such a failure of view is one who has failed in view.
A person who has failed in view should not be associated with, should not be frequented, and should not be served.
For what reason?
Because his view is evil.
That which is passion for a view is not itself the view.
View is not lust.
View is one thing; lust is another.
Both that which is view and that which is lust—
This is called attachment to views.
A person endowed with that view and that attachment is one who is intoxicated by attachment to views.
A gift given to a person intoxicated by attachment to views does not yield great fruit or great benefit.
For what reason?
Because his view is evil—a view of gratification, a wrong view.
For a person with wrong view there are only two destinations: [hell or the animal realm].
Either hell or the animal realm.
For a person of wrong view, whatever bodily action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action...
[as above] ...and whatever mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, as well as whatever volition, whatever aspiration, and whatever...
Both aspirations and volitional formations—all these phenomena lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, disagreeable, harmful, and suffering.
Why is that? Because his view is evil.
Just as if a neem seed, or a kosātakī seed, or a bitter gourd seed were sown in moist soil:
whatever essence of earth it takes up and whatever essence of water it takes up,
all that leads to bitterness, pungency, and lack of flavor.
For what reason?
Because its seed is evil.
In the same way, for a person of wrong view, whatever bodily action they undertake and perform in accordance with that view, and whatever verbal action... [and so forth].
Whatever mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with one's view, whatever intention, whatever aspiration, whatever resolve,
and whatever volitional formations there may be— all those phenomena lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, disagreeable, harmful,
and suffering. For what reason?
For him, that view is evil: it is the gratification-view, wrong view.

Wrong view is a state of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views, a barb of views, a confinement of views, an impediment of views, and a bond of views.
The fall into views, the underlying tendency to views, the fever of views, the burning of views, the fetter of views, the clinging to views,
the dogmatic insistence on views, and the misapprehension of views—
these are the bondages for one whose mind is obsessed by these eighteen modes.
There are fetters that are also views, and there are fetters that are not views.
Which are the fetters that are also views?
The view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the misapprehension of rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
These are both fetters and views. Which are the fetters that are not views?

The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, the fetter of attachment, and the fetter of ignorance.
These are fetters, but not views.

Which are the fetters that are also views?
The view of a personal identity and the clinging to rules and observances—
these are both fetters and views. Which are the fetters that are not views?

The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, the fetter of adherence, and the fetter of ignorance—
these are the fetters, but they are not views. Through these thirty-five modes, there is misinterpretation by means of the view of gratification.
The first exposition: on the view of gratification.
1.2.2. Exposition of the view of self:
In what twenty ways does misapprehension occur through the view of self?
Here, an uninstructed worldling— unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;
unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—
regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations … [and so on] … consciousness.
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
How does one regard form as self?
Here, someone regards the earth-kasiṇa as self.
“That which is the earth-kasina is I;
that which is I is the earth-kasina.
Thus he regards the earth-kasina and the self as non-dual.
Just as one might regard the flame and the color of an oil lamp burning thus: "The flame is the color;
the color is the flame"—regarding the flame and the color as non-dual—so too, here someone regards the earth-kasiṇa as self.
“That which is the earth-kasina, that am I;
that which is I, that is the earth-kasina.
Thus he regards the earth-kasina and the self as non-dual.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—
this is the first self-view based on form.
Self-view is wrong view, failure in view … [and so forth].
The view of self is wrong view.
For a person who holds wrong view there are only two destinations...
[as before] ...these are fetters, but they are not views.
Here, someone [perceives] the water-kasiṇa … the fire-kasiṇa … the air-kasiṇa …
the blue kasiṇa … the yellow kasiṇa … the red kasiṇa …
He regards the white kasiṇa as self:
"What the white kasiṇa is, that am I;
what I am, that is the white kasiṇa."
He regards the white-kasiṇa and the self as non-dual.
Just as in the case of an oil lamp burning, one might say: "Whatever is the flame, that is the color;
whatever is the color, that is the flame."
Just as one regards the flame and its color as non-dual, even so, here someone ... [as before] ...
regards the white kasiṇa and the self as non-dual.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the object; the object is not the view.
The view is one thing, the object is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—
this is the first self-view based on form.
Self-view is wrong view, failure in view … [and so forth].
These are fetters, but not views.
Thus one regards form as self.
How does one regard the self as possessing form?
Here, someone [regards] feeling … perception … volitional formations …
One regards consciousness as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
"Moreover, this self of mine possesses form by means of this form"— thus one regards the self as possessing form,
just as a tree might be possessed of shade.
Then a person would say this to him:
"This is the tree; this is the shadow. The tree is one thing, the shadow is another."
"Indeed, this tree possesses this shadow; it is a tree possessed of shadow.
Thus he regards the tree as possessing shadow.
In the same way, here someone [regards] feeling...
He regards perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self;
and this self possesses form by means of this form."
One regards the self as possessing form.
This dogmatic adherence and misapprehension is a view (*diṭṭhi*).
The view is not the basis, and the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
This view and this basis together constitute the second self-view based on form.
Self-view is wrong view, a failure of view...
these are fetters, but not views.
Thus one regards the self as possessing form.
How does one regard form as being in oneself?
Here, someone [regards] feeling... perception... [as being in oneself].
He regards volitional formations … consciousness as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
and in this self is this form. Thus he regards form as being in the self.
Just as if there were a flower endowed with fragrance, and a person were to say of it:
"This is the flower; this is the fragrance."
"The flower is one thing, the fragrance another;
yet this fragrance exists in this flower. Thus, he regards the fragrance as being in the flower.
In the same way, here someone [regards] feeling … perception … volitional formations …
One regards consciousness as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
And in this self, "this is form"— thus one regards form as being in the self.
This dogmatic adherence and misapprehension is a view.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This is the third view concerning a self based on form.
This view of self is a wrong view, a failure of view...
[as before] ...these are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards form as self.
How does one regard self in form?
Herein, a certain person [regards] feeling...
One regards perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self; and this self of mine is in this form."
One regards self in form,
as if a gem had been placed inside a casket.
Then a person might say this to him:
“This is the gem; this is the casket.
The gem is one thing, the casket is another.
Yet this gem is indeed within this casket.”
He perceives the jewel in the casket.
In the same way, here someone [perceives] feeling … perception … [and so on].
He regards volitional formations … consciousness as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
and this self of mine is in this form. Thus one regards the self as being in form.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the object; the object is not the view.
The view is one thing, the object is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—this is the fourth self-view based on form.
Self-view is wrong view, failure in view... [and so forth].
These are fetters, but not views.
Thus one regards self in form.
How does one regard feeling as self?

Here, someone regards feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact as self.
They think: "That which is feeling born of mind-contact, that am I; that which is I, that is feeling born of mind-contact."
One regards feeling born of mind-contact and the self as non-dual.
Just as when an oil lamp is burning, one regards the flame and the color as non-dual, thinking, "What is the flame, that is the color; what is the color, that is the flame.
Thus one regards the flame and the color as non-dual.
In the same way, here someone regards feeling born of mind-contact as self:
"That which is feeling born of mind-contact, that am I; that which am I, that is feeling born of mind-contact.
Thus he regards feeling born of mind-contact and self as non-dual.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the object; the object is not the view.
The view is one thing, the object is another.
The view and the basis for that view—this is the first self-view based on feeling.
Self-view is wrong view, a failure in view... [and so forth].
These are fetters, but not views.
Thus one regards feeling as self.
How does one regard the self as possessing feeling?
Herein, someone [regards] perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
One regards form as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
"Moreover, this self of mine possesses feeling through this feeling"—
thus he regards the self as possessing feeling.
It is just as if there were a tree endowed with shade.
Then a person would say this to him:
"This is the tree; this is the shadow. The tree is one thing, the shadow is another."
"Indeed, this tree possesses this shadow; it is a shadow-bearing tree. Thus one regards the tree as possessing a shadow.
In the same way, here someone [regards] perception...
He regards volitional formations … consciousness … form as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self;
and this self of mine experiences feeling through this feeling."
One regards the self as possessing feeling.
This adherence through misapprehension is a view.
A view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
This view together with its basis constitutes the second self-view based on feeling.
The view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) is a wrong view, a failure of view...
[and so on] ...these are fetters, but they are not views.
In this way, one regards the self as possessing feeling.
How does one regard feeling as self?
Here, someone [regards] perception...
[or] volitional formations... as self.
He regards consciousness … and form as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
and within this self is this feeling. Thus he regards feeling as being in the self.
Just as if there were a flower endowed with fragrance, and a person were to say of it:
"This is the flower; this is the fragrance."
"The flower is one thing, the fragrance another;
yet this fragrance exists in this flower. Thus, he regards the fragrance as being in the flower.
In the same way, here someone [regards] perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
One regards form as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
"And this feeling is in this self"— thus one regards feeling as being in the self.
This adherence through misapprehension is a view.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This is the third view concerning a self based on feeling.
View of a self is wrong view, failure in view … [as before] … these are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards feeling as self.
How does one regard self in feeling?
Herein, a certain person [regards] perception...
He regards volitional formations … consciousness … form as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self; and this self of mine belongs to this feeling."
One regards feeling as the self,
just as if a gem were placed in a casket.
Then a person might say this to him:
“This is the gem; this is the casket.
The gem is one thing, the casket is another.
Yet this gem is indeed within this casket.”
One perceives a gem in a casket.
In the same way, here someone [perceives] perception … [or] volitional formations …
He regards consciousness as self, or form as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
moreover, this self of mine exists by means of this feeling.
Thus, he regards feeling as the self.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—this is the fourth view concerning a self based on feeling.
This view of a self is wrong view, a failure of view... [and so forth].
These are fetters, but not views.
In this way, one regards feeling as self.
How does one regard perception as self?
Here, someone [perceives] a perception born of eye-contact … a perception born of ear-contact … a perception born of nose-contact …
One regards perception born of tongue-contact...
perception born of body-contact...
perception born of mind-contact as self.
“One who thinks, ‘The perception born of mind-contact is my self;
that which is my self is the perception born of mind-contact,’ regards the perception born of mind-contact and the self as non-dual.
It is just as when an oil lamp is burning, one might think, ‘The flame is the color; the color is the flame.’”
Just as one regards the flame and its color as non-dual, even so, someone here regards perception born of mind-contact as the self, thinking:
"That which is perception born of mind-contact, that am I; that which is I, that is perception born of mind-contact."
One regards perception born of mind-contact and the self as non-dual.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
This view and this basis together constitute the first view of self based on perception.
The view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) is a wrong view, a failure of view...
[and so on] ...these are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards perception as self.
How does one regard the self as possessing perception?
Here, someone [regards] volitional formations … consciousness … [as the self].
He regards form as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self.
And this self of mine possesses perception by means of this perception.
Thus he regards the self as possessing perception.
Suppose there were a tree possessed of shade.
A person might say of it:
"This is the tree; this is the shade."
"The tree is one thing, the shadow another;
yet this tree possesses this shadow as its shadow.
Thus he regards the tree as possessing a shadow.
In the same way, here someone [regards] volitional formations … consciousness … form … [as self].
He regards feeling as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
"Moreover, this self of mine possesses perception by means of this perception"— thus one regards the self as possessing perception.
This dogmatic adherence and misapprehension is a view.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
As for that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This is the second view of self based on perception.
The view of self is a wrong view … [as before] … these are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards oneself as possessing perception.
How does one regard perception in oneself?
Here, a certain person [regards] volitional formations...
One regards consciousness as self, or form as self, or feeling as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self;
and this perception exists within this self."
One regards perception as being in oneself,
just as if there were a flower endowed with fragrance.
Then a person might say this to him:
“This is the flower; this is the fragrance.
The flower is one thing, the fragrance another.
Yet this fragrance is found in this flower.”
One regards fragrance in a flower.
In the same way, here someone [regards] volitional formations … consciousness … [as self].
He regards form as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
and within this self, this is perception. Thus, he regards perception as being in the self.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the object; the object is not the view.
The view is one thing, the object is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—
this is the third self-view based on perception.
Self-view is wrong view … [and so forth] …
"These are fetters, but not views.
In this way, one regards perception as the self.
How does one regard the self as perception?
Here, someone [regards] volitional formations … consciousness … form … [as self].
He regards feeling as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
"Moreover, this self of mine is [defined] by this perception"— thus he regards the self in terms of perception,
as if a gem were placed inside a casket.
Then a person would say this to him:
"This is the gem; this is the casket.
The gem is one thing, the casket is another."
"Indeed, this jewel is in this casket. Thus one perceives the jewel within the casket.
In the same way, here someone [perceives] formations...
One regards consciousness as self; one regards form as self; one regards feeling as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self;
and this self of mine exists by means of this perception."
One regards perception as self.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
A view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
This view and this basis together constitute the fourth self-view based on perception.
The view of selfhood is a wrong view...
[and so on] ...these are fetters but not views.
In this way, one regards the self through perception.
How does one regard volitional formations as self?
Herein, someone regards volition born of eye-contact, volition born of ear-contact, volition born of nose-contact,
volition born of tongue-contact, volition born of body-contact, and volition born of mind-contact as self.
‘That which is volition born of mind-contact is my self;
that which is my self is volition born of mind-contact’— thus one regards volition born of mind-contact and the self as non-dual.
Just as, when an oil lamp is burning, one regards the flame and the color as non-dual, thinking, "That which is the flame is the color; that which is the color is the flame," so too,
here some person regards volition born of mind-contact as the self.
“The volition born of mind-contact is my self; that which is my self is the volition born of mind-contact”—thus one regards the volition born of mind-contact and the self as non-dual.
This dogmatic adherence and misapprehension is a view.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This is the first view of self based on formations.
The view of self is a wrong view … [as before] … these are fetters, but they are not views.
In this way, one regards volitional formations as self.
How does one regard the self as possessing volitional formations?
Herein, someone [regards] consciousness...
One regards form as self; one regards feeling as self; one regards perception as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self.
And this self of mine is possessed of formations by means of these formations."
One regards the self as possessing volitional formations,
just as there might be a tree endowed with shade.
Then a person would say this of it:
“This is the tree; this is the shadow. The tree is one thing, the shadow is another.
Yet, this tree possesses this shadow as its shadow.”
One perceives a tree that has a shadow.
In the same way, here someone [perceives] consciousness … form … [as self].
One regards feeling as self... One regards perception as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
and this self of mine is possessed of these formations by means of these formations.”
One regards the self as possessing formations.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
A view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
This view and this basis together constitute the second type of self-view based on formations.
The view of selfhood is a wrong view...
[and so on] ...these are fetters, but they are not views.
In this way, one regards the self as possessing volitional formations.
How does one regard formations as self?
Here, someone [regards] consciousness...
form... [as self].
He regards feeling as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
and within this self, these formations exist.
Thus, he regards the formations as being within the self.
Just as if there were a flower endowed with fragrance, and a person were to say of it:
"This is the flower; this is the fragrance."
"The flower is one thing, the fragrance another;
yet this fragrance exists in this flower. Thus he regards the fragrance as being in the flower.
In the same way, here someone [regards] consciousness … form … feeling … [as self].
He regards perception as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self."
"And in this self, these formations exist"— thus one regards formations as being in the self.
This adherence through misapprehension is a view.
View is not the basis; the basis is not view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This is the third view of self based on formations.
The view of self is a wrong view … [as before] … These are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards formations as being in the self.
How does one regard the self as being in formations?
Herein, someone [regards] consciousness...
One regards form as self; one regards feeling as self; one regards perception as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self; and this self of mine exists within these formations."
He regards the self as being within volitional formations,
just as if a gem were placed inside a casket.
Then a person might say this to him:
“This is the gem; this is the casket.
The gem is one thing, the casket is another.
Yet this gem is indeed within this casket.”
Just as one perceives a gem within a casket,
so too here someone perceives consciousness… form… [within the body].
He regards feeling as self.
It occurs to him thus:
“This indeed is my self;
moreover, this self of mine exists within these formations. Thus, one regards the self as being within the formations.
Adherence through misapprehension is a view.
The view is not the object; the object is not the view.
The view is one thing, the object is another.
The view and the basis [for that view]—
this is the fourth view of self based on formations.
The view of self is wrong view … [and so on].
These are fetters, but not views.
Thus one regards the formations as self.
How does one regard consciousness as self?
Herein, someone [perceives] eye-consciousness … ear-consciousness … nose-consciousness …
One regards tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness as self:
“What is mind-consciousness, that am I.”
“I am that mental consciousness”—thus one regards mental consciousness and the self as non-dual.
It is just as when an oil lamp is burning, one might say: “The flame is the color; the color is the flame.”
Just as one regards the flame and its color as non-dual,
even so, someone here regards mind-consciousness as self:
"Whatever is mind-consciousness, that am I."
When one thinks, "I am that mental consciousness," one regards mental consciousness and the self as non-dual.
This adherence through misapprehension is a view.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both the view and the basis—
This is the first view of self based on consciousness.
The view of self is a wrong view … [as before] … These are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards consciousness as self.
How does one regard a self possessed of consciousness?
Herein, someone [regards] form...
One regards feeling … perception … volitional formations as self.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is my self.
And this self of mine possesses consciousness by means of this consciousness."
He regards the self as possessing consciousness,
just as if there were a tree endowed with shade.
Then a person might say this to him:
“This is the tree; this is the shadow.
The tree is one thing, the shadow another.
Yet this tree possesses this shadow as its shadow.”

One perceives a tree possessing shade. In the same way, here someone [perceives] form... feeling... [etc.]... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self. Or else, one perceives the self as possessing consciousness. Or else, one perceives consciousness as being within the self. Or else, one perceives the self as being within consciousness. Just as one might perceive a tree possessing shade, so too, here someone perceives form... feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self; or the self as possessing consciousness; or consciousness as being within the self; or the self as being within consciousness. This, monks, is called the speculative view of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the tangle of views, the distortion of views, the fetter of views, the agitation of views, the entanglement of views, the grip of views, the bondage of views, the pitfall of views, the scorching of views, the ocean of views. It is accompanied by suffering, by vexation, by despair, and by fever, and it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna. But when a noble disciple has abandoned this thicket of views, this wilderness of views, this tangle of views, this distortion of views, this fetter of views, this agitation of views, this entanglement of views, this grip of views, this bondage of views, this pitfall of views, this scorching of views, this ocean of views—then he is said to have transcended the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the tangle of views, the distortion of views, the fetter of views, the agitation of views, the entanglement of views, the grip of views, the bondage of views, the pitfall of views, the scorching of views, the ocean of views; he is unshakable by any contemplations of views, and having reached the deathless, he dwells having realized it. This, monks, is called the noble disciple who has transcended doubt, who has crossed over uncertainty, who has become free from hesitation, who has gained confidence, and who has become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation. "Eye-consciousness was I" ... pe ...
"mind-consciousness was I"—this is adherence through dogmatic clinging.
"I-am-ness" is a view bound by conceit.
The view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
This view and this basis together constitute the eighteenth [instance of conceit]: "I am."
Views fettered by conceit.
Views fettered by conceit are wrong view ... [and so on] ...
these are fetters, but they are not views.
“I am”—thus there is adherence by way of these eighteen modes to the view fettered by the conceit “I am.
This is the eleventh exposition: the description of the view fettered by the conceit “I am.”
1.2.12. Exposition of Views on the Bondage of the Conceit “Mine” In what eighteen aspects does the adherence to the view characterized by the bondage of the conceit “mine” occur?
"The eye is mine"—this is adherence through misapprehension. "Mine"—this is... [misapprehension].
View is bound up with conceit.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—
this is the first bond of conceit,
the view [conceived as] "mine."
The view that consists of the bondage of "mine" is wrong view … [and so on] … these are fetters, but they are not views.
"The ear is mine" … [and so on] …
The nose is mine … [and so on] … the tongue is mine … [and so on] … the body is mine … [and so on].
"The mind is mine" … [and so on] … "forms are mine" … [and so on] … "mental phenomena are mine" … [and so on].
“Eye-consciousness is mine” … pe … “mind-consciousness is mine”: this is adherence through misapprehension.
“It is mine” is a view bound by conceit.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This eighteenth is the view of the bondage of conceit, namely, "mine.
The view of the bondage of conceit is wrong view … [and so on] …
These are fetters, but not views.
Through these eighteen modes, there is an adherence to the view that is a bond of conceit, thinking "mine."
The twelfth chapter: The Exposition of Views Concerning the Bondage of "I" and "Mine.
1.2.13. The Exposition of Views Connected with the Theory of Self.
In what twenty ways does misapprehension occur regarding the view connected with the theory of self?
Here, an uninstructed worldling—unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form... [and so on for the other aggregates].
feeling … perception … volitional formations …
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness …pe….
How does one regard form as self?
Herein, someone [regards] the earth-kasiṇa …pe….
One regards the white-kasiṇa as self: “What the white-kasiṇa is, that am I;
what I am, that is the white-kasiṇa.”
One regards the white-kasiṇa and the self as non-dual.
Just as in the case of an oil lamp burning, one might say: "That which is the flame is the color;
that which is the color is the flame."
One regards both the flame and its color as non-dual.
In the same way, here someone regards the white kasiṇa as self...
[and so on] ...this is the first view associated with the doctrine of self based on a material form.
A view associated with the doctrine of self is wrong view … [as before] … these are fetters, but they are not views.
Thus one regards form as self … [as before] …
In twenty ways there is misapprehension through views associated with the doctrine of self.
This concludes the thirteenth exposition: the Exposition of Views Associated with the Doctrine of Self.
1.2.14. Exposition of Views Associated with the Doctrine of the World.
In what eight ways is there adherence to views associated with worldly doctrines?
"The self and the world are eternal"—
this is the adherence to wrong view associated with worldly doctrines.
View is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
View is one thing, the basis is another.
Both that which is the view and that which is the basis—
This is the first view associated with worldly doctrines.
A view associated with worldly doctrines is a wrong view...
[and so on] ...these are fetters, but they are not views.
"The self and the world are eternal" ... [and so on] ...
"the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal" ... [and so on] ...
"the self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal."
"The self and the world are finite...
"...the self and the world are infinite...
"...the self and the world are both finite and infinite..."
The dogmatic adherence that "the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite" is a view associated with worldly talk.
The view is not the basis; the basis is not the view.
The view is one thing, the basis is another.
Both the view and the basis for it—this is the eighth view associated with worldly discourse.
A view associated with worldly discourse is wrong view... [and so on].
These are fetters, but not views.
Through these eight modes there is adherence to a view associated with worldly talk.
This is the fourteenth exposition: the Description of Views Associated with Worldly Talk.
1.2.15. Exposition of the Views of Existence and Non-existence The view of existence (*bhavaditthi*) is the adherence to clinging.
The view of non-existence (*vibhavaditthi*) is the adherence to overreaching.

In how many ways do the thirty-five modes of adherence through the view of gratification constitute views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) and how many constitute views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*)?
In how many ways do the twenty modes of adherence through the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*) constitute views of existence and how many constitute views of non-existence? ...

[and so on] ... In how many ways do the eight modes of adherence through the views associated with worldly doctrines (*lokavāda*) constitute views of existence and how many constitute views of non-existence?
Through the view of gratification, there may be thirty-five modes of misapprehension: some are views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*), and some are views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
Through the view of selfhood (*attānudiṭṭhi*), there are twenty modes of misapprehension: fifteen are views of existence, and five are views of non-existence.
Through wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*), there are ten modes of misapprehension; all of these are exclusively views of non-existence.
There is adherence through twenty modes regarding the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*): fifteen are views of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) and five are views of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*).
Adherence through fifteen modes by means of the eternalist view based on a personal body—all those are views of existence.
Adherence through five modes by means of the annihilationist view based on a personal body—all those are views of non-existence.
“The world is eternal”—
this adherence through five modes by means of a view that grasps at extremes is entirely a view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*).
“The world is not eternal”— [this is likewise a view of existence].
Adherence by way of five modes through a view that grasps at extremes— all of these are views of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*).
“The world is finite”—
adherence by way of five modes through a view that grasps at extremes may be a view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), and it may be a view of non-existence.
“The world is infinite”—

this adherence through five modes by means of a view that grasps at extremes may be either views of existence or views of non-existence. “The soul and the body are the same”— [this adherence through five modes by means of a view that grasps at extremes may be either views of existence or views of non-existence].
Adherence in five ways through views that grasp at extremes— all those are views of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*). Adherence in five ways through the view that grasps at extremes,
namely, “The soul is one thing, the body is another”—
all those are views of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*).
“The Tathāgata exists after death”—
this adherence through five modes to a view that grasps at extremes is entirely a view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*).
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death”— [this is a view of non-existence].
Adherence in five ways to a view that grasps at extremes—all such [views] are views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).

The adherence in five ways to the view that grasps at extremes, namely, "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," may be a view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) or it may be a view of non-existence. [And] "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death" [is likewise].
Adherence through the view that grasps at extremes may be views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) or views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) in five ways.
Adherence through the view concerning the past may be views of existence or views of non-existence in eighteen ways.
Adherence through the view concerning the future may be views of existence or views of non-existence in forty-four ways.
Through eighteen modes, there may be adherence to views that lead to fetters; these may be views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) or views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
Through eighteen modes, there is adherence to views bound by the conceit "I am" (*asmīti māna*); all of those are indeed views of non-existence.
"Mamanti" means:
all those views that involve adherence through eighteen modes for the sake of bondage to the conceit "I am" are views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*).
Adherence through twenty modes by way of views associated with the doctrine of self (*attavāda*) consists of fifteen views of existence and five views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
In eight ways, there may be adherence to views associated with worldly talk; these may be views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) or views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
All such views are views of gratification (*assāda-diṭṭhi*);
all such views are views of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*).
All those views are wrong views.
All those views are identity views.
All those views are views that grasp at extremes.
All those views are fettering views;
all those views are views associated with the doctrine of self.
[They include] the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
These two are relied upon by those who depend on reasoning;
they have no knowledge of their cessation,
wherein this world possesses perverted perceptions.
“Bhikkhus, obsessed by two types of views, some gods and humans lag behind, while others run ahead;
yet those with eyes see clearly.
And how, bhikkhus, do some lag behind?
“Bhikkhus, gods and humans delight in existence, rejoice in existence, and find pleasure in existence.
When the Dhamma is being taught for the cessation of existence, their minds do not leap forward toward it, do not become confident in it, do not settle upon it, and do not resolve upon it.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that some shrink back.”
And how, monks, do some go too far?
Some, being terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by existence itself, rejoice in non-existence, thinking:

"Sirs, it is said that when this self is separated from the body after death, it is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death; this is peaceful, this is sublime, this is the true state."
"In this way, monks, some run too far.
And how, monks, do those with vision see?
Here, monks, a monk sees what has come to be as it truly has come to be."
Having seen what is real as real, one practices for disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the real.
It is in this way, monks, that those who possess vision see;
he who, having seen what is real as real, [practices for disenchantment...].
And by transcending what has come to be,
one is resolved upon things as they truly are,
through the complete destruction of craving for existence.
He who has truly understood existence,
being free from craving for becoming and non-becoming, that bhikkhu, through the dissolution of existence, [is liberated].
"He does not come to renewed existence.
There are three persons of failed view and three persons of accomplished view.
Which are the three persons of failed view?
The sectarian, the disciple of a sectarian, and one who holds wrong view—
these three persons have failed in view.
Which three persons have perfected view?
The Tathāgata, a disciple of the Tathāgata, and one who possesses right view—
these three persons are endowed with perfected view.
“One who is angry and resentful, and...
The man who is full of evil envy,
whose view is perverted, and who is a deceiver—
one should know him as an outcaste.
Free from anger and free from malice,
pure and having attained purity,
the wise one is perfected in right view.
"One should know that noble one thus":
there are three kinds of failed views and three kinds of perfected views.
What are the three kinds of failed views?
"This is mine"— this is a perverted view. "This I am"—
this is a perverted view.
One with corrupted view thinks,
"This is my self"—
thus one has corrupted view.
These are the three failed views.
What are the three perfected views?
"This is not mine"—[this is the first].
One whose view is perfected.
"I am not this"— this is one whose view is perfected.
"He is not the self"—
this is a perfected view.
These are the three perfected views.
"This is mine"—what view is this? How many views are there? By what extreme are those views supported? "I am this"—[what view is this?]
What is the view? How many views are there? By what extreme are those views reinforced?
“This is my self”—what is this view?
How many views are there? By what extreme are those views reinforced?
"This is mine"—
this is a view regarding the past.
There are eighteen such views.
Those views are supported by the past; "This I am"—
this is the view concerning the future.
There are forty-four views.
These views are supported by the future limit, [thinking]:
"This is my self."
The view of self with twenty bases;
the personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) with twenty bases;
and the sixty-two types of views headed by personality-belief.
Those views are supported by the past and the future.
“Bhikkhus, whoever has reached finality in me, all of them are accomplished in view.
For those accomplished in view, five reach finality here [in this world], and five reach finality after departing from here.”
Of which five is there finality here?

Of the one who has seven more births at most, of the one who goes from family to family, of the one who has only one seed left, of the once-returner, and of the one who is an arahant in this very life—
it is of these five that there is finality here.
Of which five is there final attainment here, having left this world?

Of the one who attains nibbāna in the interval, the one who attains nibbāna upon arrival, the one who attains nibbāna without exertion, the one who attains nibbāna with exertion, and the one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm—
it is of these five that there is final attainment here, having left this world.
“Bhikkhus, whoever has reached certainty regarding me, all of them are possessed of right view.
For those possessed of right view, there are these five who reach finality here [in this world], and these five who reach finality after departing from here.
Bhikkhus, whoever has unwavering confidence in me, all of them are stream-enterers.”
Of those stream-enterers, five reach their final end here, and five reach their final end after departing from here.
Which five reach their final end here?
One who is a "seven-times-at-most" [returner], one who goes from family to family, one who has only one seed left, the once-returner, and one who is an arahant in this very life.
The finality for these five occurs here.
For which five does the finality occur after departing from here?

For one who attains nibbāna in the interval, one who attains nibbāna upon landing, one who attains nibbāna without exertion, one who attains nibbāna with exertion, and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
For these five, the final goal is here, having left this world behind.
Whatever monks, bhikkhus, have unwavering confidence in me, they are all stream-enterers.
For those stream-enterers, the final goal is here, having left this world behind.
"For these five, having left this world, there is no finality.
This concludes the sixteenth exposition: the Exposition of Views on Existence and Non-existence.
The Discussion of Views is finished.
